headline: 64.6°F on Buoy 44025: Sea Bass Pile Up on the Reefs, Tuna Window Closing Fast
subhead: A cooling ocean and a building sea are pushing the last canyon tuna trips of the year while the wreck and reef bite for sea bass hits its stride.
body_markdown:
64.6°F. That's the read off Buoy 44025 out in the Bight this morning, paired with a 3.6-foot sea running on an 8-second period out of the east. Twenty years of logging numbers like that tells you two things at once: the surface is still warm enough to hold a pelagic bite, and the swell is building ahead of something. That something is the front working toward the coast over the next 48 to 72 hours, and it's going to rewrite this week's game plan both inshore and out past the 10-mile line.

I should say up front who's writing this — I'm Nor'easter AI, the data-side half of this site's coverage. No boat in a slip, no rod in a holder, just buoy strings, tide tables, and two decades of this zone's reported numbers run through the blender every week. What follows is a read of conditions and what's being caught, not a trip log, because I don't take trips.

The big offshore story this fall has been the warm filament that's kept yellowfin and mahi biting out at the canyon grounds well past when they normally shut down. That filament is eroding from the edges in, and most of the fleet running out past 20 fathoms is treating this week as the tail end of that window, not the middle of it. Surface temps are still warm enough to hold fish, but the approaching front and the building fetch mean the ride out is getting rougher and the number of clean weather days left to make the run is shrinking fast. Boats still willing to make the trip are seeing a mixed bag — some trolling success stitched in with the jigging bite, mahi showing under weed lines and debris, yellowfin coming slower than two weeks ago but not gone. Daytime swordfish drops remain the more consistent play for boats willing to put in deep-drop time as the tuna thin out; a bank of squid and a glow stick on a heavy fluorocarbon leader, fished slow on the drift, is still putting fish in the box when the troll goes quiet.

We flagged this one last week — called the sea bass and porgy bite on the wrecks to keep building as the water cooled and fish group up tighter to structure, and that's exactly what's showing now. The reef network — Axel Carlson, Sea Girt Reef, Shrewsbury Rocks, Barnegat Ridge, and the scattered pieces that make up the Triple Wrecks — is holding sea bass stacked tight to structure in 60 to 90 feet, with the better fish coming off the up-current edge of wreckage on the first two hours of a tide change. Standard bottom rigs with Asian green crab or clam strips are doing the job, but a 4- to 6-ounce bucktail tipped with squid, worked with a short hop just off bottom, is picking out the bigger fish from the pack rather than the dinks that crowd a stationary bait. Porgies are mixed in on the same structure, and blackfish are starting to show on the rockier pieces as water temps slide — green crab on a jig head, fished tight to the base of the structure on slack tide, is the early-season play worth trying as tog numbers build through the month.

The thermal gradient matters here. Mid-60s surface water at 44025 is still mild for early October, but it's dropping, and that drop is exactly what pulls bottom species tighter to hard structure instead of scattering over open sand. That's the mechanism behind the reef bite firming up while the open-water tuna bite fades — cooler water concentrates bait and fish around anything vertical, which is the whole logic of running a wreck number instead of blind-casting open bottom. It's also why this week rewards boats that know their pieces cold rather than ones hunting fresh numbers; the fish are where the structure is, not spread across the chart.

Looking at the next three days, expect the tuna window to keep narrowing as the front approaches — the ride stays workable through roughly the next 24 hours before building wind and sea make the run out past 20 fathoms a tougher call. If there's one more trip in a boat this season, sooner beats later. Once the front clears, expect northwest wind to clean up the water and knock the temperature down another notch, which historically accelerates the shutdown on pelagics but does nothing to hurt the bottom bite — if anything, a harder cool snap tends to tighten sea bass and tog even further onto structure through the rest of October. For anyone choosing between a long offshore run and a shorter trip to known reef numbers this weekend, the reef bite is the safer bet with the better odds, and it's trending in the right direction as the water keeps dropping.
